title: Courting AI: Understanding AI in Courts
pub: Court Manager (National Association for Court Management), Vol. 38 #4, Fall 2024
author: Roger Rand

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source broadly aligns with the cluster’s view that AI should reallocate work—automating administrative tasks while staff retain justice-critical responsibilities—and that claimed benefits must not be mistaken for validated capability. Its contribution is illustrative rather than empirical: the court-management applications are explicitly predictive and potentially inaccurate, so it supports cautious, use-specific assessment without establishing realised value, verification adequacy or general competence.
qs: - **Purposes and Responsibilities:** AI can help courts fulfill their fundamental purposes by streamlining administrative tasks, allowing court staff to focus on more critical responsibilities like ensuring justice and fairness.

kp.k: Court leadership prioritised institutional AI education
kp.d: Rand reports that COSCA, NACM and the Joint Technology Committee made AI a priority in 2023. NACM commissioned a guide to educate court professionals about AI and court uses; its first version, published in 2024, contained 109 pages. This describes an institutional educational response rather than evidence of widespread operational adoption.
qs: Last year both the Conference of State Court Administrators (COSCA) and NACM, along with the Joint Technology Committee (JTC), made artificial intelligence a priority topic.
The NACM Board approved the creation of a guide to help educate its membership about artificial intelligence and its use in courts.
The first version of the guide published in 2024 ended up being 109 pages long.

kp.k: Generative AI produced role-specific professional reading paths
kp.d: The editors uploaded the guide to ChatGPT 4.0 and explained its intended readership, obtaining seven suggested reading paths for court administrators, finance directors, human resource directors, judges, CORE-interested readers, supervisors and managers, and technologists. Rand presents this as an actual use of generative AI to make substantial professional education material more navigable for time-constrained court personnel, without reporting an effectiveness assessment.
qs: The guide editors uploaded a copy of the guide to a generative AI resource, ChatGPT 4.0, and asked it to create reading paths for the different sectors of court professionals.
ChatGPT was provided with an explanation of who was expected to read the guide.
As a result, ChatGPT generated seven different suggested reading paths.

kp.k: Competency mapping demonstrates generation, not validated court applications
kp.d: Rand reproduces a Copilot conversation dated 8/22/2024 linking AI to the 13 NACM CORE competencies. He reports that the chatbot corrected his erroneous competency name using the NACM website and drew on NCSC material, producing an answer in seconds. He explicitly cautions that the generated applications and competency links may be inaccurate or may not represent actual court uses; the examples are illustrative chatbot output, not measured findings.
qs: When it generated an answer, it corrected the title of that competency based on what it found on the NACM website.
It formulated this answer in seconds!

kp.k: Administrative automation could redirect court staff toward complex work
kp.d: In his demonstration prompt, Rand proposes automating simple tasks so employees can concentrate on more complicated case filings, with improved data accuracy. The reproduced Copilot answer extends this possibility to data entry, case management, scheduling, notifications, document management, resource allocation and bottleneck detection. These are proposed task changes and benefits, not documented productivity outcomes or staffing reductions.
qs: for instance, ai can help automate simple tasks so that court employees can focus on more complicated case filings.
AI can automate data entry and case management tasks, reducing human error and increasing data accuracy.
AI can optimize case scheduling and resource allocation, ensuring that cases move through the system efficiently.
AI can manage routine operational tasks such as scheduling, notifications, and document management.

kp.k: Chatbot proposes AI-supported training and workforce management
kp.d: The Copilot response suggests adaptive learning to identify court staff knowledge gaps and recommend training, alongside resume screening and data-driven employee performance and development insights. These suggestions concern court personnel and management; the article does not establish their implementation or evaluate their effects.
qs: AI can provide personalized learning experiences for court staff through adaptive learning platforms.
These platforms can identify knowledge gaps and recommend targeted training programs.
AI can assist in recruitment by screening resumes and identifying the best candidates.
It can also help in performance management by providing data-driven insights into employee performance and development needs.

kp.k: Public-facing AI benefits remain illustrative possibilities
kp.d: The reproduced Copilot answer proposes easier public access to court information and decisions, chatbots answering common questions, public-sentiment analysis and social-media monitoring. It associates these uses with transparency, approachability and responsiveness, but provides no evidence of realised public-trust gains or reduced unmet civil legal need.
qs: AI can enhance transparency by providing the public with easy access to court information and decisions.
Chatbots can assist in answering common queries, making the court system more approachable and understandable.
AI-driven tools can analyze public sentiment and feedback, helping court leaders understand and address public concerns more effectively.
Social media monitoring tools can also help manage the court’s public image.

kp.k: Chatbot suggests AI-assisted governance and resource planning
kp.d: Copilot's illustrative competency mapping proposes ethical-violation monitoring, decision support for leaders, forecasting for strategic planning, automated IT maintenance and security-threat detection, and spending analysis for budgeting. These broad claims—including the assertion that AI can ensure ethical compliance—belong to the reproduced chatbot response and remain subject to Rand's explicit warning about its accuracy and applicability.
qs: AI can ensure compliance with ethical standards by monitoring court activities and flagging potential ethical violations.
AI can support leadership by providing data-driven insights and predictive analytics, helping leaders make informed decisions.
AI can analyze trends and forecast future needs, aiding in strategic planning.
AI can enhance IT management by automating routine maintenance tasks, detecting security threats, and ensuring that court systems are up-to-date and secure.
AI can optimize budget allocation by analyzing spending patterns and identifying areas for cost savings.

kp.k: Human oversight is necessary for useful court AI
kp.d: Rand warns that generative chatbots predict answers and can invent them when lacking factual grounding. Referring to an NCSC Tiny Chat warning about the “Sea of Junk,” he recommends keeping humans in the loop so court AI developments are useful. The article supplies no measured hallucination rate or detailed verification protocol.
qs: When using generative AI chatbots, it is important to understand that they use technology that predicts (guesses) what should be produced as the desired answer.
If the chatbot does not have access to facts upon which to base the answer, it makes the answer up.
There are many potential benefits for the use of AI in courts, but we need to keep humans in the loop to make sure that what we develop is useful and not junk.

kp.k: Rapid AI change requires more frequent professional guidance
kp.d: Rand argues that rapid technological change and emerging court applications make NACM's usual six-to-ten-year guide revision interval unsuitable for AI. The JTC workgroup and NACM Communications Committee therefore established twice-yearly updates, illustrating a move toward more continuously maintained professional guidance.
qs: Existing NACM guides are typically revised every six-to-ten years.
It is not just a fear, but a reality that anything we publish about the understanding and use of AI in courts needs to be updated more frequently than NACM’s other guides.
The JTC workgroup and the NACM Communications Committee devised a process to update the guide twice per year.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Rand presents generative AI as an aid to court-professional education and administration, while distinguishing demonstrated document-navigation uses from speculative court applications.
pts.d: Rand reports that the guide editors used ChatGPT 4.0 to produce seven audience-specific reading paths through the 109-page guide. He also states that generative AI can help professionals navigate the NACM CORE curriculum and suggest applications to court administration. In his demonstration, he reports that a chatbot corrected a competency-name typo and assembled an answer using website information within seconds. His prompt proposes automating simple tasks so employees can focus on more complicated filings and improving data accuracy. The reproduced Copilot answer extends these possibilities to scheduling, resource allocation, public information, operational tasks, public sentiment analysis, personalized education, recruitment and performance management, ethics monitoring, leadership, strategic planning, IT security, and budgeting. These extensions are explicitly chatbot-generated suggestions, not independently established findings or unqualified predictions by Rand. Rand's own broader claims are that AI offers potential court benefits, requires humans in the loop to avoid useless output, and changes sufficiently quickly to require more frequent professional-guidance updates.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of the guide team's practical experience and Rand's illustrative chatbot interaction, rather than measured court-service outcomes.
pts.d: The reading-path claim rests on a reported use of ChatGPT 4.0 by the editors. The typo-correction and rapid-answer claims rest on Rand's account of his own experiment; the document identifies the reproduced answer as a Copilot conversation dated August 22, 2024. Rand says the chatbot consulted NACM and NCSC information, and the reproduced answer includes source links. Those references concern court-management competencies and do not establish that the proposed AI applications have produced the stated operational benefits. The article provides no quantitative evaluation, benchmark, controlled study, or documented deployment outcomes for the suggested improvements to accuracy, efficiency, public trust, ethics, staffing, or budgeting. The claim of rapid technological change is supported by the workgroup's experience of sharing innovation-related materials nearly every day.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article reports uses in 2024, gives no forecast deadline for wider court applications, and conditions usefulness on factual grounding and human involvement.
pts.d: The first guide and the reported reading-path exercise belong to the 2024 publication context; the Copilot demonstration is dated August 22, 2024. The broader administrative applications are framed as present possibilities, not adoption forecasts with specified deadlines. Rand explicitly cautions that chatbot answers are predictive, can be fabricated without access to facts, and may neither describe actual court uses nor correctly map applications to the competencies. His human-in-the-loop requirement frames AI as assistance rather than unrestricted autonomous substitution. Because of rapid change, NACM plans twice-yearly updates instead of the usual six-to-ten-year guide revision cycle, with revisions in December and June for publication in January and July.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are court professionals and court users, rather than law firms or commercial legal-service markets.
pts.d: The demonstrated reading paths target court administrators, finance directors, human resource directors, judges, CORE-interested readers, supervisors and managers, and technologists, helping busy professionals locate relevant educational material. Rand's automation example concerns court employees redirecting attention from simple tasks to more complicated filings. The chatbot-generated possibilities concern administrative leaders, staff, recruitment candidates, IT teams, and finance personnel, alongside members of the public seeking court information or greater transparency. Benefits to public trust and the administration of justice remain proposed outcomes, not measured effects. NACM, its Communications Committee, and the JTC are also affected through the ongoing work of reviewing and updating AI guidance.
